blocks.text: Design Search Autocomplete: Suggestions Before You Finish Typing

The second great interview classic: a system that guesses your search before you finish typing — a trie with precomputed top-k answers, sharded and cached until a million lookups a second feel like nothing.
The day search started answering before the question

September 8, 2010. Marissa Mayer is on stage typing into a search box — slowly, theatrically. Behind her, the results page is changing while she types, before she presses Enter, before she even finishes the word. The feature was called Google Instant, and Mayer called it "a fundamental shift in search." The room understood the demo instantly, because everyone in it had felt the friction it removed: type, stop, wait, read, retype. Instant made the page keep up with your fingers.

Here's the part people forget: Instant had two halves. One half re-ran the search on every keystroke and repainted the results — that half died in July 2017, when Google removed it because of mobile. The other half — the dropdown of predicted searches under the box — never died. It's on your phone right now. It survived because it wasn't a gimmick; it was a data structure with an opinion about what you're about to say, and it was right often enough to save the world real time.

That dropdown is this lesson's system. It looks like the simplest feature on the internet. It is quietly one of the hardest: it must answer on every keystroke, for every user, in less time than the user needs to type the next letter — and what it answers with is a ranked summary of what billions of people have asked before you. This lesson designs the serving half: how the answer is ready before the question. The next lesson designs the learning half: where the answers come from, and how the system keeps them fresh — and keeps them from embarrassing you.
Why this matters

"Design search autocomplete" (interviewers also call it typeahead) is the second great interview classic, the natural sequel to the URL shortener. The shortener tested whether you can mint and look up keys. Autocomplete tests everything else at once:
A data structure under a latency gun. You will reach for a trie — a tree where each step down adds one character, so every path spells a prefix — and then discover the trie is the easy part.

A read path that out-traffics the product it serves. Every search becomes roughly ten suggestion requests. The tail wags the dog: your lookup tier absorbs about 10× the search engine's own query rate. (The math is below; check it.)

A serving tier that may never improvise. At this request rate and this latency budget, there is no time to compute an answer per keystroke. The answers must already exist. Almost every design decision in this lesson is that sentence, applied.
If the URL shortener was a coat-check counter, autocomplete is the friend who finishes your sentences. Let's meet the friend properly.
First, clarify the problem
The system does exactly one thing:

Complete the query. The user has typed a prefix — desi — and the system returns the about 10 most likely full queries that start with it: design patterns, design a url shortener, designer bags… The user picks one (or ignores the list and keeps typing).
Everything else is a follow-up to park, exactly as you parked analytics on the shortener:
Actually running the search? No. We produce the query text; some other system executes it. Our API is GET /suggest?prefix=desi → a ranked list of strings.

How fast? This is the requirement that designs the system: suggestions must feel instant. Human perception gives us the number — under about 0.1 seconds a system feels like it's reacting instantaneously, and 1.0 seconds is the limit for keeping the user's flow of thought uninterrupted. (Jakob Nielsen's response-time limits, unchanged since 1993.) Our budget: once a request fires, the full round trip, network included, lands in under about 100 ms, which leaves the server only tens of milliseconds to do its work. Bloomberg's question-answering autocomplete reports completions typically "in no more than 60 to 80 milliseconds," spelling correction included.
How big? Fix the scale now, as always: let's say 5 billion searches a day on our engine, worldwide, many languages. Hold that number; the math section spends it.

Personalized? Park it — with a note. Real systems blend in your own history (Google's help page lists language, location, trending interest, and your past searches as the factors its predictions use ). The next lesson shows where the per-user list merges in; this lesson serves global popularity first.
Fresh? A suggestion list frozen last month misses this morning's breaking news. Freshness is the next lesson's whole subject; here, just register that the serving tier must leave a door open for it.
Picture a friend who finishes your sentences
This lesson's running analogy: a friend who has heard every sentence ever started, and finishes yours before you can.

You know this friend. You say "do you know where the—" and they're already saying "—station, two blocks left." How do they do it? Not by magic, and not by searching a filing cabinet mid-conversation. Two of their habits carry this whole lesson:

They've heard it all before. Every finished sentence anyone has said in their hearing is tallied somewhere in their memory. Suggestions in our system are likewise previous searches, counted — the counting itself is the next lesson.

For every half-sentence, they keep a shortlist ready. They don't compose your ending on the spot; for common openings, the likely endings are pre-ranked in their head, and out one comes. That's our precomputed top-k list per prefix — the k highest-ranked completions for that prefix, k = 10 in this design — and it's the design's beating heart.
(The friend's other two habits — keeping up with the times, and having tact — run the next lesson.)
Keep the friend in mind. Every component below is one of their habits, mechanized.
Back-of-envelope math: the tail that wags the dog
Start from the scope: 5 billion searches a day. The course's rounding rule: a day ≈ 100,000 seconds (the estimation lessons show why this rounding is honest).
The searches themselves: 5,000,000,000 ÷ 100,000 ≈ 50,000 searches/sec on average; call peak 2×, so about 100,000/sec. Respectable, not terrifying.

The suggestion requests: here's the multiplication that designs the system. A user typing a query fires a request per keystroke once the prefix is a couple of characters long. Say the average query is about 15 characters and the client asks on about 10 of those keystrokes. Then every search becomes about 10 lookups: 50,000 × 10 = 500,000 lookups/sec average, about 1,000,000/sec at peak. Read that again. The suggestion tier — the decorative dropdown — must absorb ten times the request rate of the search engine it decorates, and each answer is due in tens of milliseconds. This is the whole design problem in one line: a million tiny lookups a second, each one essentially free, or the feature is a liability.

One sizing note: those rates are the load that actually arrives at the fleet — counted after the client's debounce has already suppressed mid-burst keystrokes (the about 10 requests per search above are requests that fired, not raw keystrokes). Size for these.

The corpus: suggestions come from queries people actually ran. Suppose we keep the top 2 billion distinct queries by popularity (the tail beyond that is typed too rarely to be worth suggesting — and a Google spokesperson said about 15 percent of daily searches are brand new (via CNET, December 2016), so the tail is genuinely endless). Store each as about 25 bytes of text plus a count and timestamps, about 40 bytes all-in: 2 × 10⁹ × 40 B ≈ 80 GB. That is small — it fits in RAM across a modest fleet. The corpus is not the problem. The corpus organized for prefix lookup is the problem, and it's the next section.

The prefix explosion (why you can't cheat): the lazy design is a hash map from every possible prefix to its suggestion list. Count the keys: 2 billion queries × about 15 prefixes each ≈ 30 billion prefix entries. No. The entries must share structure — every query starting how to must live under the same how to path, stored once. Data structures that share prefixes have a name, and it's the next section's entire subject.
The crux: a trie that answers, not searches

A trie (from retrieval) is a tree where each edge is a character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Walk down d → e → s → i and you're standing on every query that starts with desi; the subtree under you is exactly your candidate set. The structure is old and it's still the answer — but a bare trie only tells you which queries match. Serving needs the top 10 by rank, per prefix, in microseconds. So the production trick, the sentence this lesson exists to teach:

Precompute the answer at every node. Each trie node stores the top-k (k = 10) suggestion IDs for its prefix, ranked offline. Serving is then: walk the prefix, read the list, done — no sorting, no scanning, no ranking at request time.

The cost moves to build time, where it belongs: a batch process recomputes every node's list from the query counts. The read path becomes a memory walk — one step per prefix character — plus one small list read: microseconds of work, which is how you afford a million of them a second at peak. The research-grade version of this idea — squeezing the structure into a succinct index so it fits in memory at web scale — is Bast and Weber's SIGIR 2006 paper — the succinct-index approach to autocomplete search.
A pocket-sized piece of the trie, for three queries that start alike:
Two refinements keep the trie honest at scale:

Compression. A naive node-per-character tree wastes memory on long unique suffixes (the tail of design a url shortener has one tenant). A radix (Patricia) trie collapses single-child chains into one edge labelled with the whole string — same answers, a fraction of the nodes.

IDs, not strings. Nodes store suggestion IDs; a side table maps ID → query text and its current score. Rebuilds then shuffle small integers instead of copying strings, and the ranking layer can re-score without touching the tree's shape.
Ranking, in one paragraph (the next lesson gives it a chapter)

The node's top-10 is ordered by a score computed offline: decayed frequency (how often the world asked this, recent days weighted up, log-scaled so giants don't crowd out the merely popular), plus a trending boost for queries suddenly running far above their baseline. And one component is not a score at all: a policy gate — whatever the numbers say, a suggestion flagged as hateful, explicit, or dangerous does not ship. Frequency proposes; policy disposes. Why the gate is load-bearing, and what happens on the one famous occasion it was missing, is the next lesson's opening story.
Sharding the trie, caching the obvious

Shard by prefix. The 80 GB corpus splits across a fleet by the opening characters of the prefix: in the baseline split, one shard owns every a prefix, another every b, and so on. A request routes by its prefix to exactly one shard — no scatter-gather (sending the same request out to many shards and merging their replies): the prefix itself picks the shard, so there is no fan-out and no merge step. The trap is skew: prefixes are not created equal. a, how, and whatever this morning's headline starts with will hammer their shards while qzx idles. Defences, in order of escalation: shard by two characters — separate shards own aa, ab, ac, … (676 = 26 × 26 pairs in a simplified 26-letter alphabet; a real multilingual fleet normalizes text and buckets by opening-character ranges across scripts), replicate the hot shards read-only, and let the cache absorb the celebrity prefixes entirely.

Cache in three places, because the math begs for it. Query popularity is brutally skewed — a small head of prefixes serves an outsized share of all keystrokes (exactly how outsized varies by engine; the steep-head, long-tail shape doesn't). So:

At the edge / in the serving tier: the top about 100,000 prefixes' lists, cached in memory. Assume one cached list runs about 350 bytes (ten short query strings plus overhead): 100,000 × 350 B = 35,000,000 B ≈ about 35 MB — pocket change that absorbs a large share of the firehose before it reaches a trie.

In the client: debounce. The client waits about 150 ms after the last keystroke before firing, so a keystroke superseded inside that window never becomes a request at all — mid-burst, most keystrokes are superseded, and only a pause lets a request out. And tag every request with a sequence number: responses that arrive after a newer one are discarded, so a slow answer for des never overwrites the fresh one for desi. Stale pixels are worse than no pixels.

Negative space, briefly: a prefix with no completions (qzx…) is a real answer — cache it too, with a short TTL (time to live: how long the cached "no completions" answer may be reused before it's thrown away and asked again), or every fast typist re-asks the fleet the same unanswerable question.
The full walkthrough: one keystroke, end to end
A user types desi, one keystroke at a time, on a healthy system:

Keystrokes d, de, des: the user hesitates slightly between characters — just long enough for two requests to escape: #39 for de, #40 for des. (The first lone letter fires nothing; one character has no useful completions, and the debounce window swallows it.)

desi lands, about 150 ms of quiet: the client fires GET /suggest?prefix=desi tagged sequence #41. The answers to #39 and #40 are still in flight — when they land, their sequence tags mark them stale and they are discarded unpainted.
Edge: the request hits the nearest serving point. desi is a head prefix, so its list is likely in the edge cache — a hit ends the journey here.

Trie shard: on a cache miss, the request routes by prefix to the shard owning de, which walks d→e→s→i in its in-memory radix trie and reads the node's stored top-10 IDs. No disk. No ranking. A list read.
Response: ten strings, a few hundred bytes, back to the client — which checks the sequence tag (still the newest? good) and paints the dropdown.
Budget check against the 100 ms promise:
Leg, Cost, Note
Debounce wait, about 150 ms, before the request fires, Deliberate, and outside the 100 ms budget: the price of not firing per keystroke. The budget clock starts when the request fires
Network round trip, about 20–50 ms, Geography, not engineering, sets most of this
Cache hit or trie walk, about 1–10 ms, In-memory on both paths — that's the design working
Response after firing, tens of ms, Inside the about 100 ms feel-instant budget

The system feels instant not because any single part is heroic, but because no part is allowed to be slow: the expensive thinking — counting, ranking, screening — all happened before the keystroke. Where it happens is the next lesson.

One term the diagrams below use: a snapshot is one complete, self-contained built copy of the trie — the tree, its top-k lists, the ID table — stamped with a version number (v42 below) naming which copy a node is serving. Nodes swap snapshots atomically: the old copy keeps answering until the new one is fully loaded, then a pointer flips. A half-loaded index is never served.
Takeaways

Autocomplete is a lookup service wearing a search costume: about 10 lookups per search means about 10⁶ lookups/sec at peak , each due in tens of milliseconds — so all expensive thinking happens offline, and the read path only walks and reads.
The data structure is a trie with the top-k answers precomputed at every node; the all-prefixes hash map dies by arithmetic ( about 30 billion keys ) and per-request ranking dies by latency.

Serving stays honest at scale by sharding the trie by prefix, replicating and caching the skewed head (edge cache, client debounce, cached empty results), and tagging every response with a sequence number so stale answers never paint.
The snapshot the fleet serves is built, not live-edited — versioned, swapped atomically. Building it well is a whole second system, and it's the next lesson.
